planting.note: Divide rooted offsets or root stem cuttings in warm, humid conditions and keep soil evenly moist but never waterlogged.

directions: Grow this low Amazonian understory plant in bright, indirect light or deep shade, since its quilted olive-green leaves with purple undersides scorch quickly in direct sun. Keep the humidity high and the compost consistently moist, misting or using a pebble tray if indoor air is dry. Propagate easily from stem cuttings laid on damp soil, and pinch growing tips occasionally to keep the clump compact rather than leggy. It makes an excellent terrarium or paludarium specimen thanks to its tolerance of low light and high humidity.

planting.note: Divide offsets from the rosette and set shallowly in a well-draining, humus-rich mix kept out of direct sun.

directions: This Brazilian rainforest-floor native forms a flat rosette of velvety, dark green leaves marked with a silvery central stripe and deep maroon undersides and hairs. Keep it in deep shade with warmth and steady humidity, since the fuzzy foliage is prone to rot if water sits on the leaf surface. Water from below or along the soil line and let the top layer dry slightly between waterings to avoid crown rot. Small lavender-pink three-petaled flowers appear briefly above the foliage, but the plant is grown primarily as a foliage specimen for terrariums and shaded plantings.

planting.note: Root stem-tip cuttings in moist, warm potting mix and transplant once new leaves form; keep out of direct sun at all times.

directions: A tropical American gesneriad grown for its glossy, quilted bronze-green leaves that flush almost chocolate-brown in lower light, this plant thrives in the same warm, shaded, humid conditions favored by African violets and other gesneriads. Small tubular yellow-throated flowers appear sporadically among the foliage but are secondary to the leaf display. Pinch stems regularly to prevent the naturally sprawling growth from becoming lanky, and avoid cold drafts or direct sun, both of which quickly damage the soft leaves. It is a popular terrarium and vivarium plant because it tolerates the low light and high humidity those environments provide.

planting.note: Plant scaly rhizomes shallowly in rich, moist, well-draining soil after the danger of cold has passed and keep in bright shade.

directions: This Andean gesneriad grows from small scaly rhizomes into a mounding plant covered with slender, bright orange-red tubular flowers over soft, fuzzy foliage. Grow it in filtered or dappled shade with consistent moisture, since the thin leaves wilt quickly in dry conditions or strong sun. After flowering tapers off in cooler months, the plant can die back to its rhizomes and should be kept on the dry side until new growth resumes. It is well suited to hanging baskets or shaded border edges where its long bloom season and hummingbird-attracting flowers can be appreciated up close.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Start dormant rhizomes (tuberous scales) shallowly in moist seed-starting mix once temperatures stay warm, and keep in shade until shoots emerge.

directions: This small Mexican and Central American gesneriad grows from underground scaly rhizomes into a compact mound of soft, velvety leaves topped with small purple-pink tubular flowers. It prefers constant warmth, shade, and humidity through the growing season, then goes fully dormant and should be kept nearly dry once foliage dies back in cool weather. Repot and restart the rhizomes the following spring to keep the clump vigorous and floriferous. Its diminutive size and tolerance of low light make it a favorite for terrariums and windowsill gesneriad collections.

planting.note: Divide offsets at the base of the clump and replant in rich, moisture-retentive soil, keeping the crown just at soil level.

directions: Larger and coarser than the common houseplant peace lily, this South American aroid produces broad, glossy, lance-shaped leaves and a narrow, often twisted, creamy-white spathe surrounding its flower spike. It tolerates deep shade and swampy, constantly moist soil in its native habitat, making it useful for wet shaded spots where many other foliage plants would struggle. Give it warmth and high humidity year-round, since it does not tolerate temperatures near freezing or prolonged drought. Division is the most reliable way to propagate it, as named clones rarely come true from seed and offsets form readily around the base of a mature clump.
